details:
**Tilting at windmills**
The most famous episode: Don Quixote charges a row of windmills, believing they are giants, despite Sancho Panza's protests. His lance catches in a sail and he is thrown, and he blames an enchanter for turning the giants into windmills. It has become the standard giveaway and the source of the phrase "tilting at windmills."

**The Knight of the White Moon (Samson Carrasco)**
The bachelor Samson Carrasco, a neighbor, tries to cure Don Quixote by defeating him in a joust. He fails the first time as the Knight of the Mirrors, then succeeds in Barcelona disguised as the Knight of the White Moon. He makes Quixote promise to return home and give up knight-errantry for a year. Quixote falls ill with a fever, renounces the books of chivalry, and dies as plain Alonso Quixano.

**Sancho Panza**
Don Quixote's plump, practical peasant neighbor, who becomes his squire in exchange for the promise of an island to govern. He rides his donkey Dapple (which the convict Gines de Pasamonte steals at one point) and dubs his master the "Knight of the Sorrowful Countenance."

**Dulcinea del Toboso**
The lady to whom Don Quixote dedicates his deeds. She is really a peasant farm girl, Aldonza Lorenzo, from the village of El Toboso. He attacks merchants from Toledo who refuse to swear to her matchless beauty. In Part Two, Sancho passes off a coarse peasant girl as Dulcinea and convinces Quixote that she has been enchanted.

**Rocinante**
Don Quixote's broken-down old nag, which he names as a proper knight's steed. In the final joust, the Knight of the White Moon's horse is "much swifter than Rocinante."

**The burning of the library**
Alonso Quixano's brain "dries up" from "so little sleeping and so much reading" of chivalric romances. While he sleeps, the priest (the curate) and Master Nicholas the barber, helped by his niece and housekeeper, examine and burn his library, sparing a few books such as Amadis of Gaul. They then wall up the room, and his niece tells him that an enchanter riding a dragon from a cloud carried the books away.

**The blanket tossing and the Balsam of Fierabras**
At an inn he believes is a castle, Don Quixote brews the magical healing Balsam of Fierabras, which makes both him and Sancho violently sick. When Quixote leaves without paying, claiming knights-errant never pay at inns, the guests toss Sancho up and down in a blanket.

**The Helmet of Mambrino**
Don Quixote attacks a traveling barber and seizes his brass shaving basin, believing it to be the enchanted golden Helmet of Mambrino from chivalric legend. He wears the basin on his head.

**Cide Hamete Benengeli**
The fictional Moorish (Arab) historian whose manuscript the narrator claims to have found in Toledo and had translated. The novel is presented as a translation of his work.

**The Duke and Duchess, Barataria, and the 3,300 lashes**
In Part Two, a bored Duke and Duchess who have read Part One play elaborate pranks on the pair. They make Sancho governor of the "island" of Barataria, where he judges cases wisely. A servant dressed as Merlin declares that Sancho must whip himself 3,300 times to disenchant Dulcinea.

**Part Two, the "third sally," and Avellaneda's false sequel**
The novel was published in two parts, in 1605 and 1615. Part Two describes Quixote's third sally and has characters who have read Part One. It was partly written to answer a spurious "Second Part" published by "Avellaneda," which Cervantes mocks in the prologue with the story of a madman who inflates a dog through a hollow reed. At the end, Quixote's will disinherits his niece if she marries a man who reads books of chivalry.

**Marcela and Grisostomo**
The student-shepherd Grisostomo dies for love of the beautiful shepherdess Marcela. At his funeral, the traveler Vivaldo compares the knightly life to a monk's and reads Grisostomo's "Song of Despair." Marcela appears and defends her freedom, arguing that she had no obligation to love him just because he loved her.

**The galley slaves and Master Pedro's puppet show**
Don Quixote frees a chain of galley slaves, who stone him when he orders them to report to Dulcinea. Their leader, Gines de Pasamonte, later reappears as the puppeteer Master Pedro, who has a fortune-telling ape. Quixote suspects the ape of a pact with the Devil and destroys the puppet show, mistaking the puppet Moors for real enemies.

**Cardenio, the wineskins, and "The Man Who Was Recklessly Curious"**
In the Sierra Morena, Quixote meets Cardenio, a ragged man driven mad by love for Luscinda. At the inn, the priest reads aloud the interpolated tale "The Man Who Was Recklessly Curious," in which Anselmo has his friend Lothario test his wife Camilla's fidelity. The reading is interrupted when a sleepwalking Quixote slashes wineskins, thinking he is fighting a giant.

**Literary responses: Borges, Kafka, and Lennox**
Jorge Luis Borges wrote "Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote," about a man who rewrites the novel word for word, and the essay "Partial Magic in the Quixote." Franz Kafka's parable "The Truth about Sancho Panza" calls Quixote Sancho's "demon." Charlotte Lennox's 1752 novel The Female Quixote features Arabella as a female counterpart.
